subject: botany_2
question_text: Define transformation in Griffith's experiment. Discuss how it helps in the identification of DNA as genetic material.

insider_note: Four injections, four results. Set them out as four numbered lines — an examiner marking this looks for the fourth one, where the mice die.

steps.label: What transformation is
steps.margin_note: Definition, the worker, the year, the organism. Seven lines.
lines: TRANSFORMATION is the genetic alteration of a
cell caused by taking up genetic material
directly from its surroundings, through the
cell membrane.
Frederick Griffith showed it in 1928, working on
STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE, the bacterium
that causes pneumonia.
steps.why: Something has to physically pass from the dead cells into the living ones, and identifying what that something is became the whole question of the next twenty years.
common_mistakes: Saying transformation needs contact between two live cells. That is CONJUGATION.
Naming the wrong organism. Griffith worked on Streptococcus pneumoniae.
steps.memory_tip: Something passes from the dead cells into the living ones.

steps.label: The two strains
steps.margin_note: Both strains with all three features each: colony, capsule, virulence.
lines: Griffith grew the bacterium on a culture medium
and found TWO strains:
1. S-type: forms SMOOTH colonies, HAS a capsule,
and is VIRULENT (it causes disease).
2. R-type: forms ROUGH colonies, has NO capsule,
and is NON-VIRULENT.
steps.why: The capsule is what makes the S strain deadly, and it is also what makes the two strains tell apart by eye — so one visible difference tracks one lethal one.
common_mistakes: Saying R-type is virulent. S-type is the virulent one.
Leaving out the capsule. It is what makes S-type smooth and virulent.
steps.memory_tip: Smooth has a coat and kills; rough has none and does not.

steps.label: The four injections
steps.margin_note: All four injections with their results. The recovery of live S-type is the key line.
lines: 1. LIVE S-type injected: the mice got pneumonia
and DIED.
2. LIVE R-type injected: the mice SURVIVED.
3. HEAT-KILLED S-type injected: the mice
SURVIVED.
4. HEAT-KILLED S-type MIXED with live R-type:
the mice DIED, and LIVE S-type bacteria were
recovered from their bodies.
steps.why: Injections 2 and 3 are the controls: each alone is harmless, so only their combination can explain the death in injection 4.
common_mistakes: Giving only the fourth injection. The first three are the controls that make it mean something.
Forgetting that LIVE S-type was recovered from the dead mice. That recovery is the whole result.
steps.memory_tip: Two harmless things mixed became deadly.

steps.label: The conclusion
steps.margin_note: Name the transforming principle, say it was heritable, and credit the identification correctly. Getting that credit right is what the last mark is for.

lines.text: Something from the dead S cells transformed the
live R cells, and it was heritable

lines: Griffith concluded that the R-strain cells had
been TRANSFORMED by something released from the
heat-killed S-strain cells.
He called it the TRANSFORMING PRINCIPLE.
The transformed cells bred true, so the
transferred material was the GENETIC material.
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty later showed the
transforming principle is DNA.
steps.why: The transformed bacteria stayed S-type in every later generation, which is what shows the transferred material was genetic rather than a passing chemical effect.
common_mistakes: Saying Griffith proved DNA is the genetic material. He did NOT — he showed a transforming principle existed. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identified it as DNA.
Leaving out the heritability. It is what makes it genetic.
steps.memory_tip: Griffith found the parcel; Avery opened it.
